MUQATIL:76:1-3/r1.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:76:1-3/r1.speaker: author
MUQATIL:76:1-3/r1.claim: The unmentioned period was 21,000 years, or three sevenths, after heaven and earth were made.

MUQATIL:76:1/r1.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:76:1/r1.speaker: author
MUQATIL:76:1/r1.claim: The unnamed human is Adam: for 21,000 years, or three seventh divisions, after heaven and earth were created, no one remembered him because he did not yet exist.

MUQATIL:76:1/r2.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:76:1/r2.speaker: author
MUQATIL:76:1/r2.claim: Jinn inhabited earth, then disobeyed God and harmed one another; God sent an angel tribe called Jinn, including Iblis, whose name was al-Harith, to expel them beyond earth.

MUQATIL:76:1/r3.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:76:1/r3.speaker: author
MUQATIL:76:1/r3.claim: The expelled jinn were driven into darkness behind a barrier mountain where the sun sets; between it and Mount Qaf lay a year-long distance of darkness and still water.

MUQATIL:76:1/r4.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:76:1/r4.speaker: author
MUQATIL:76:1/r4.claim: Iblis and his host purified earth and worshipped God; when God announced a human successor, the angels anticipated corruption and bloodshed from the jinn they had seen, not from knowledge of the unseen.

MUQATIL:76:1/r5.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:76:1/r5.speaker: author
MUQATIL:76:1/r5.claim: God sent Gabriel for soil from beneath the Kaaba, the earth's surface layer; mixed with water and left until it stank, it became sticky clay on top and dark mud below.

MUQATIL:76:1/r6.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:76:1/r6.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
MUQATIL:76:1/r6.claim: The Prophet said people made from the sticky clay were the people of the right, while those from dark mud were the people of the left.

MUQATIL:76:1/r7.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:76:1/r7.speaker: author
MUQATIL:76:1/r7.claim: Imru al-Qays ibn Abis al-Kindi and the Jewish Malik ibn al-Dayf disputed Adam's creation; Malik claimed the Torah placed it at the creation of heaven and earth, and revelation refuted him.

FARRA:v3p213#2/r1.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v3p213#2/r1.speaker: author
FARRA:v3p213#2/r1.claim: Here hal is affirmative and means “it has indeed come”; a question such as “Did I admonish you?” presupposes it happened, unlike a rhetorical denial.

FARRA:v3p213#2/r2.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v3p213#2/r2.speaker: author
FARRA:v3p213#2/r2.claim: “He was not a mentioned thing” means he existed but was not mentioned, from his creation out of clay until the spirit was breathed into him.

MAJAZ:v2p279/r1.author: Abū ʿUbayda Maʿmar b. al-Muthannā
MAJAZ:v2p279/r1.speaker: author
MAJAZ:v2p279/r1.claim: Hal atā means indeed it has come, not a question; Abū Bakr's saying about wishing an ordeal had ended supports this idiomatic use.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p336/r1.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p336/r1.speaker: قتادة
ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p336/r1.claim: Qatada says Adam was the last of God's creation to be created.

IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p502#2/r1.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p502#2/r1.speaker: المفسرون
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p502#2/r1.claim: The commentators take hal atā as “it has indeed come.”

TAB-FULL:v23p530/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v23p530/r1.speaker: بعض أهل التأويل
TAB-FULL:v23p530/r1.claim: Some interpreters say the unmentioned interval was forty years, when Adam's clay form had been fashioned but had not yet received a soul; he existed bodily but was not yet remembered.

ZAJJAJ:v5p257/r1.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v5p257/r1.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v5p257/r1.claim: “Has there come” means “has there not come”; one reading concerns a person who was dust and clay, not mentioned before the spirit was breathed into him.

ZAJJAJ:v5p257/r2.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v5p257/r2.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v5p257/r2.claim: Alternatively, the verse concerns all people, who passed through sperm, clot, and morsel stages before becoming mentionable.

ZAJJAJ:v5p257/r3.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v5p257/r3.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v5p257/r3.claim: Hal atā also has the completed sense “it has come upon the human.”

IBNABIHATIM:v10p3390/r1.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3390/r1.speaker: قتادة
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3390/r1.claim: Qatadah says humanity came after a period in which people were not mentioned, and that no later creature of God was known beyond humankind.

NAHHAS:v5p95/r1.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v5p95/r1.speaker: أهل التفسير
NAHHAS:v5p95/r1.claim: Exegetes take the first al-insān as Adam, though it may mean humanity; the second refers only to humanity as a species.

NAHHAS:v5p95/r2.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v5p95/r2.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v5p95/r2.claim: Nuṭfah is a little water held in a vessel.

SULAMI:v2p363/r1.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v2p363/r1.speaker: جعفر
SULAMI:v2p363/r1.claim: Has there ever been a time when God was not remembering the human being?

SULAMI:v2p363/r2.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v2p363/r2.speaker: أبو سعيد القرشي
SULAMI:v2p363/r2.claim: The human is called insan because he forgot the covenants and pledges.

SULAMI:v2p363/r3.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v2p363/r3.speaker: بعضهم
SULAMI:v2p363/r3.claim: People find companionship in different things: ordinary people in one another, the elect in God's speech and worship, saints in divine wonders, and the greatest in God alone.

THALABI:v10p93#3/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p93#3/r1.speaker: author
THALABI:v10p93#3/r1.claim: The first human, Adam, passed forty years between Mecca and Taif before receiving the spirit; during that time he was unmentioned, unknown, and not yet identified by name or purpose.

THALABI:v10p93#3/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p93#3/r2.speaker: عمر
THALABI:v10p93#3/r2.claim: Umar heard someone recite the verse and said he wished the condition of not being mentioned had continued.

THALABI:v10p93#3/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p93#3/r3.speaker: عون بن عبد الله
THALABI:v10p93#3/r3.claim: Awn ibn Abd Allah reports a similar wish after a man recited the verse before Ibn Masud.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p161/r1.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p161/r1.speaker: ابن عباس ومقاتل والكلبي ويحيى بن سلام
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p161/r1.claim: They classify Surat al-Insan as Meccan.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p161/r10.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p161/r10.speaker: يحيى بن سلام
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p161/r10.claim: Not being mentioned means not being mentioned among created beings, although known to God.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p161/r11.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p161/r11.speaker: الفراء وقطرب وثعلب
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p161/r11.claim: The human was an unrecognized shaped body of earth and clay, with no known name or purpose, then became mentioned when the spirit was breathed into him.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p161/r12.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p161/r12.speaker: مقاتل
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p161/r12.claim: The word order is advanced and delayed: the sense is that a period came when the human was not mentioned, since humanity was created after all animals.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p161/r2.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p161/r2.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p161/r2.claim: Others classify only verses 23 through the end as Meccan and the preceding part as Medinan.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p161/r3.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p161/r3.speaker: الفراء وأبو عبيدة
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p161/r3.claim: هل here can mean قد, making the sentence a statement that a period did come upon humanity.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p161/r4.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p161/r4.speaker: ابن عيسى
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p161/r4.claim: Alternatively, هل retains its interrogative force.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p161/r5.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p161/r5.speaker: قتادة والسدي وعكرمة
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p161/r5.claim: The human here may be Adam, created after the heavens, earth, and everything between them, at the end of the sixth day, Friday.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p161/r6.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p161/r6.speaker: ابن عباس وابن جريج
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p161/r6.claim: Alternatively, the human here means every human being.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p161/r7.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p161/r7.speaker: ابن عباس
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p161/r7.claim: The period may be forty years before the spirit was breathed into Adam while he lay between Mecca and Taif; Abu Salih transmits this from Ibn Abbas.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p161/r8.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p161/r8.speaker: ابن عباس
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p161/r8.claim: Another report gives forty years as clay, forty as altered mud, and forty as dried clay, with Adam's creation complete after 120 years before the spirit was breathed in; al-Dahhak transmits it.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p161/r9.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p161/r9.speaker: ابن عباس
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p161/r9.claim: The period may instead be an unspecified time with no fixed limit.

QUSHAYRI:v3p373/r1.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v3p373/r1.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v3p373/r1.claim: The basmala describes God as eternally one in majesty and sovereignty, with unchanging, sacred, and everlasting attributes.

QUSHAYRI:v3p373/r2.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v3p373/r2.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v3p373/r2.claim: The verse can mean a time passed when humanity had no significance or worth.

QUSHAYRI:v3p373/r3.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v3p373/r3.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v3p373/r3.claim: One account says Adam's body lay between Mecca and Ṭāʾif forty years, then remained clay and molded clay for forty years each, completing his creation in 120 years.

QUSHAYRI:v3p373/r4.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v3p373/r4.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v3p373/r4.claim: An inward reading asks whether any moment passed without God remembering, preserving, and newly protecting the person.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p5#4/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p5#4/r1.speaker: ابن عباس ومقاتل والمفسرون وأهل المعاني
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p5#4/r1.claim: They take hal ata as an affirmative statement meaning that a time did indeed come over the human.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p5#4/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p5#4/r2.speaker: الأخفش
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p5#4/r2.claim: Hal can mean qad in this verse and in the question about the Overwhelming Event, just as a speaker may ask about something known to have happened.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p5#4/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p5#4/r3.speaker: المبرد
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p5#4/r3.claim: Here hal means qad, and he cites the question about the adversaries as another non-interrogative use.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p5#4/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p5#4/r4.speaker: سيبويه
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p5#4/r4.claim: Hal can be used for a purpose other than asking a question.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p5#4/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p5#4/r5.speaker: الكسائي
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p5#4/r5.claim: Hal can be an interrogative, its normal function, a negation, or mean qad.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p5#4/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p5#4/r6.speaker: الفراء
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p5#4/r6.claim: He reads the clause as a statement meaning qad ata; hal can introduce either a statement or a denial, and here it confirms what has happened.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p5#4/r7.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p5#4/r7.speaker: أبو إسحاق
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p5#4/r7.claim: He says hal is not interrogative and cites Abu Bakr's wish that Adam's unmentioned interval had continued without offspring or their trials; reports also attribute this wish to Umar and Ibn Masud.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p5#4/r8.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p5#4/r8.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p5#4/r8.claim: The reported wish makes sense only if hal is declarative: a real question would call for yes or no, whereas this wish answers a statement.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p7/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p7/r1.speaker: جماعة من المفسرين
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p7/r1.claim: They identify the human in this verse as Adam.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p7/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p7/r2.speaker: الكلبي
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p7/r2.claim: The interval was forty years while Adam lay before the spirit was breathed into him.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p7/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p7/r3.speaker: عطاء عن ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p7/r3.claim: Adam remained forty years as clay and forty as shaped dark clay, making his formation complete after 120 years.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p7/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p7/r4.speaker: ابن مسعود
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p7/r4.claim: He adds forty years as dust to Ibn Abbas's account, making Adam's formation complete after 160 years.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p7/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p7/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p7/r5.claim: Adam was not mentioned in either heaven or earth.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p7/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p7/r6.speaker: الفراء
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p7/r6.claim: Adam existed but was not mentioned from the time God created him until the spirit was breathed into him; al-Zajjaj gives a similar explanation.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p7/r7.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p7/r7.speaker: الزجاج
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p7/r7.claim: He also allows the phrase to mean humankind in general, who began as sperm, then clots, then tissue, until becoming something mentioned.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:76:1-3/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:76:1-3/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:76:1-3/r1.claim: One reading concerns Adam: forty years passed while he was a clay body, not remembered or known; alternatively, all people were nonexistent before becoming remembered.

TABRISI:76:1-10#4/r1.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:76:1-10#4/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
TABRISI:76:1-10#4/r1.claim: A transmitted chronology places al-Insan among the surahs revealed in Medina, after al-Rahman.

TABRISI:76:1-10#4/r2.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:76:1-10#4/r2.speaker: عكرمة والحسن بن أبي الحسن البصري
TABRISI:76:1-10#4/r2.claim: Their reported sequence puts the opening of al-Insan among the revelations in Medina.

TABRISI:76:1-10#4/r3.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:76:1-10#4/r3.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
TABRISI:76:1-10#4/r3.claim: Ali reports that the Prophet described each surah's reward in revelation order and likewise places al-Insan in the Medinan sequence.

TABRISI:76:1-10#4/r4.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:76:1-10#4/r4.speaker: author
TABRISI:76:1-10#4/r4.claim: The Prophet's reported total is 114 surahs, 6,236 verses, and 321,250 letters; only the fortunate learn the Quran and God's friends maintain its recitation.

TABRISI:76:1-10#4/r5.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:76:1-10#4/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
TABRISI:76:1-10#4/r5.claim: The report adds that a surah's opening revealed in Mecca was written there, with later additions made in Medina.

TABRISI:76:1-10#5/r1.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:76:1-10#5/r1.speaker: author
TABRISI:76:1-10#5/r1.claim: The author rejects the sectarian argument that a Medinan narrative proves this surah is fabricated because the surah is Meccan; he says he clarifies the truth against hostility to the Prophet's family.

TABRISI:76:1-10#5/r10.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:76:1-10#5/r10.speaker: سعيد الحداد
TABRISI:76:1-10#5/r10.claim: Abu Ja'far distinguishes being mentioned in divine knowledge from being mentioned in creation.

TABRISI:76:1-10#5/r2.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:76:1-10#5/r2.speaker: author
TABRISI:76:1-10#5/r2.claim: The question means “has indeed come” or “did there not come”; it is a reportative question about a time when the human was not mentioned.

TABRISI:76:1-10#5/r3.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:76:1-10#5/r3.speaker: الزجاج
TABRISI:76:1-10#5/r3.claim: The human existed as dust and clay but was not a mentioned thing until the spirit was breathed into him.

TABRISI:76:1-10#5/r4.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:76:1-10#5/r4.speaker: الجبائي
TABRISI:76:1-10#5/r4.claim: The gentle rhetorical question makes an unbeliever recognize that he once did not exist and therefore has a creator who brought him into being.

TABRISI:76:1-10#5/r5.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:76:1-10#5/r5.speaker: الحسن وقتادة وسفيان والجبائي
TABRISI:76:1-10#5/r5.claim: They identify the human as Adam, the first person given that name.

TABRISI:76:1-10#5/r6.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:76:1-10#5/r6.speaker: أبو مسلم
TABRISI:76:1-10#5/r6.claim: Abu Muslim takes “the human” generically, referring to humankind as a class.

TABRISI:76:1-10#5/r7.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:76:1-10#5/r7.speaker: author
TABRISI:76:1-10#5/r7.claim: One view says Adam's clay body lay for forty years before the spirit was breathed into it, unmentioned in heaven and earth.

TABRISI:76:1-10#5/r8.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:76:1-10#5/r8.speaker: ابن عباس
TABRISI:76:1-10#5/r8.claim: A report from Ibn Abbas says Adam's creation was completed after 120 years.

TABRISI:76:1-10#5/r9.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:76:1-10#5/r9.speaker: زرارة
TABRISI:76:1-10#5/r9.claim: Abu Ja'far explains that the human was a thing but was not mentioned.

TABRISI:76:1-10#6/r1.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:76:1-10#6/r1.speaker: عبد الأعلى مولى آل سام
TABRISI:76:1-10#6/r1.claim: Abu Abd Allah gives the same interpretation as the preceding report: the human was a thing but not mentioned.

TABRISI:76:1-10#6/r2.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:76:1-10#6/r2.speaker: حمران بن أعين
TABRISI:76:1-10#6/r2.claim: Abu Ja'far says the human was a determined thing but had not yet been brought into formed existence.

TABRISI:76:1-10#6/r3.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:76:1-10#6/r3.speaker: author
TABRISI:76:1-10#6/r3.claim: These reports support that the nonexistent is known and can be called a thing, even when it is not mentioned.

TABRISI:76:1-10#6/r4.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:76:1-10#6/r4.speaker: author
TABRISI:76:1-10#6/r4.claim: If “human” means humankind, it describes a person unknown before birth, then developing in the father's loins and mother's womb until birth.

TABRISI:76:1-10#6/r5.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:76:1-10#6/r5.speaker: author
TABRISI:76:1-10#6/r5.claim: Another interpretation says scholars were unknown, then God made them renowned through knowledge during life and after death.

TABRISI:76:1-10#6/r6.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:76:1-10#6/r6.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
TABRISI:76:1-10#6/r6.claim: After hearing the verse, Umar wished Adam had remained as he was, without children who would be tested.

TABRISI:76:1-10/r9.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:76:1-10/r9.speaker: author
TABRISI:76:1-10/r9.claim: Dahr is the passage of night and day; its plurals include adhur and duhur.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p427#2/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p427#2/r1.speaker: الفراء
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p427#2/r1.claim: Hal means qad here: the verse reports that a time did come, rather than asking a question; interrogative hal can also prompt an admission.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p427#2/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p427#2/r2.speaker: الجمهور
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p427#2/r2.claim: The human is Adam, and the time was the forty years when he was shaped from clay before the spirit was breathed into him.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p427#2/r3.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p427#2/r3.speaker: ابن عباس وابن جريج
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p427#2/r3.claim: Alternatively, al-insān means all people and the time is their development as a sperm-drop, clot, and morsel of flesh.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p427#2/r4.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p427#2/r4.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p427#2/r4.claim: The human was something, but was not yet mentioned or known.

QURTUBI-FULL:76:1-2/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:76:1-2/r1.speaker: مقاتل
QURTUBI-FULL:76:1-2/r1.claim: Muqatil proposes reordered syntax: a period passed when the human was unremembered because humanity was created after all animals and no animal afterward.

QURTUBI-FULL:76:1-2/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:76:1-2/r2.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:76:1-2/r2.claim: Another view means Adam’s descendants and the nine months of pregnancy, when the embryo is an insignificant clot and morsel.

QURTUBI-FULL:76:1-2/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:76:1-2/r3.speaker: أبو بكر
QURTUBI-FULL:76:1-2/r3.claim: Abu Bakr wished the period before Adam was remembered had continued, so people would not be born and tested.

QURTUBI-FULL:76:1-2/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:76:1-2/r4.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
QURTUBI-FULL:76:1-2/r4.claim: Umar likewise heard someone recite the verse and said, “If only it had finished.”

QURTUBI-FULL:76:1/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:76:1/r1.speaker: الكسائي والفراء وأبو عبيدة
QURTUBI-FULL:76:1/r1.claim: These grammarians take hal as qad; al-Farra says it may mark denial or a report, and here it is a report, while another view treats it as a question meaning “it came.”

QURTUBI-FULL:76:1/r10.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:76:1/r10.speaker: محمد بن الجهم عن الفراء
QURTUBI-FULL:76:1/r10.claim: Ibn Jahm transmits al-Farra’s view that Adam existed but was not yet remembered.

QURTUBI-FULL:76:1/r11.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:76:1/r11.speaker: قتادة ومقاتل
QURTUBI-FULL:76:1/r11.claim: Some take the negation literally: Adam did not yet exist or have a name among creatures; Qatada says humanity was created recently and no creature came after it.

QURTUBI-FULL:76:1/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:76:1/r2.speaker: قتادة والثوري وعكرمة والسدي
QURTUBI-FULL:76:1/r2.claim: They identify the human in the verse as Adam, a view also transmitted from Ibn Abbas.

QURTUBI-FULL:76:1/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:76:1/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
QURTUBI-FULL:76:1/r3.claim: Ibn Abbas says Adam lay between Mecca and Taif for forty years before the spirit was breathed into him.

QURTUBI-FULL:76:1/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:76:1/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
QURTUBI-FULL:76:1/r4.claim: Another report gives forty years each as clay, dark mud, and shaped clay, completing Adam after 120 years; Ibn Masud adds forty years as earth, totaling 160.

QURTUBI-FULL:76:1/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:76:1/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
QURTUBI-FULL:76:1/r5.claim: A report from Ibn Abbas says the period’s length is unknown.

QURTUBI-FULL:76:1/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:76:1/r6.speaker: ابن عباس
QURTUBI-FULL:76:1/r6.claim: Al-Dahhak transmits from Ibn Abbas that “not remembered” means Adam was neither in heaven nor on earth.

QURTUBI-FULL:76:1/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:76:1/r7.speaker: الفراء وقطرب وثعلب
QURTUBI-FULL:76:1/r7.claim: They say Adam was an unrecognized shaped body of earth and clay until the spirit entered him, after which he became known and remembered.

QURTUBI-FULL:76:1/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:76:1/r8.speaker: يحيى بن سلام
QURTUBI-FULL:76:1/r8.claim: Yahya ibn Sallam says Adam was not remembered among creation, although he was remembered by God.

QURTUBI-FULL:76:1/r9.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:76:1/r9.speaker: القشيري
QURTUBI-FULL:76:1/r9.claim: Another interpretation takes remembrance as rank and honor, which Adam gained when God made him a vicegerent and entrusted him with what the heavens and mountains declined.

BAYDAWI-FULL:76:1-2/r1.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:76:1-2/r1.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:76:1-2/r1.claim: هل أتى is a confirmatory, expectant question and means ‘indeed’; its origin is أهل, supported by a poetic line.

BAYDAWI-FULL:76:1-2/r2.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:76:1-2/r2.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:76:1-2/r2.claim: A finite stretch within unbounded time passed when the human was not yet known as a human, like an element or drop; the clause describes either الإنسان or حين. Human may be generic or Adam before his descendants.

NASAFI-FULL:v4p302#2/r1.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v4p302#2/r1.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v4p302#2/r1.claim: The human is Adam, who spent forty years as shaped clay before the spirit was breathed into him; his name and intended role were unknown.

NASAFI-FULL:v4p302#2/r2.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v4p302#2/r2.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v4p302#2/r2.claim: “A time passed over him” cannot describe nonexistence, and “not mentioned” is a circumstantial accusative describing the human as then unknown.

QASHANI:76:1-2/r1.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:76:1-2/r1.speaker: author
QASHANI:76:1-2/r1.claim: The human existed in divine knowledge and in reality through the eternal spirit, but was unmentioned among people while in the unseen world, unknown to those in the visible world.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p357/r10.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p357/r10.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p357/r10.claim: ‘The human’ most likely means humanity: the interval is nonexistence or embryonic development through successive stages until a person can be addressed, with no renown during that period.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p357/r11.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p357/r11.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p357/r11.claim: Another view identifies the human as Adam and the interval as the time before his spirit was breathed into him.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p357/r12.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p357/r12.speaker: ابن عباس
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p357/r12.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas says Adam remained clay for forty years, then shaped clay for forty, then stinking mud for forty, completing his creation in 120 years.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p357/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p357/r3.speaker: الجمهور
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p357/r3.claim: The majority consider the surah Meccan; Mujahid and Qatada call it Medinan, while Hasan and ʿIkrima say it is Medinan except the command not to obey a sinner or unbeliever.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p357/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p357/r6.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p357/r6.claim: The surah’s connection to the previous one is evident and needs no elaboration.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p357/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p357/r7.speaker: ابن عباس وقتادة
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p357/r7.claim: They take hal here to mean qad (‘already’), although hal with a nominal clause cannot mean qad and with a verb it usually marks a direct question.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p357/r8.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p357/r8.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p357/r8.claim: The explanation connects hal to an original ahl form with its hamza elided; a poem asking ‘Did they see us?’ is offered as evidence.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p357/r9.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p357/r9.speaker: أبو بكر وعمر
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p357/r9.claim: When the verse was recited to Abu Bakr, or according to another report Umar, he wished the state of being uncreated and unaccountable had lasted.

SAMIN-DURR:76:1#2/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:76:1#2/r1.speaker: الشاعر
SAMIN-DURR:76:1#2/r1.claim: A cited poem uses the preposition ba where ‘an’ would normally occur, offered as evidence for combining different particles with overlapping meaning for emphasis.

SAMIN-DURR:76:1#2/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:76:1#2/r2.speaker: الشاعر
SAMIN-DURR:76:1#2/r2.claim: Another poem repeats the same preposition in two forms, reinforcing the author’s point that repetition may emphasize a meaning even when the forms differ.

SAMIN-DURR:76:1#2/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:76:1#2/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:76:1#2/r3.claim: Al-Zamakhshari did not add the condition that the clause be verbal; the author says this omission is harmless because ‘qad’ does not directly govern nominal clauses.

SAMIN-DURR:76:1#2/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:76:1#2/r4.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:76:1#2/r4.claim: The clause ‘lam yakun’ is more clearly a circumstantial from ‘al-insan’; the alternative makes it an adjective of ‘hin’ with an understood pronoun referring to that time.

SAMIN-DURR:76:1/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:76:1/r1.speaker: الشيخ
SAMIN-DURR:76:1/r1.claim: The Shaykh takes ‘hal’ as an ordinary question about the remarkable event of a long age passing over a human who was nothing mentioned; the author calls this interpretation problematic.

SAMIN-DURR:76:1/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:76:1/r2.speaker: مكي
SAMIN-DURR:76:1/r2.claim: Makki reads ‘hal’ as a confirmatory question addressed to resurrection’s denier: he must admit a long period without people, so the One who created after nonexistence can restore them after death.

SAMIN-DURR:76:1/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:76:1/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:76:1/r3.claim: The author agrees that the confirmatory question is the correct account; a direct, ordinary question of this kind should not be attributed to God.

SAMIN-DURR:76:1/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:76:1/r4.speaker: الزمخشري
SAMIN-DURR:76:1/r4.claim: Al-Zamakhshari says ‘hal’ can equal ‘qad’ only in a question, yielding ‘has there indeed come’; the question conveys confirmation and ‘qad’ conveys nearness.

SAMIN-DURR:76:1/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:76:1/r5.speaker: الشاعر
SAMIN-DURR:76:1/r5.claim: The cited line ‘Ahl ra’ana’ is offered as evidence that interrogative ‘hal’ can mean ‘qad’ in an interrogative construction.

SAMIN-DURR:76:1/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:76:1/r6.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:76:1/r6.claim: On this reading, the human had been an unremembered, unmentioned thing; ‘hal’ can stand for ‘qad’ only with a spoken or understood question, though some omit this restriction.

SAMIN-DURR:76:1/r7.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:76:1/r7.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:76:1/r7.claim: Some reject ‘hal’ as equivalent to ‘qad’ and construe the poetic example as two semantically overlapping particles used together for emphasis despite their different wording.

SAMIN-DURR:76:1/r8.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:76:1/r8.speaker: الزمخشري
SAMIN-DURR:76:1/r8.claim: Al-Zamakhshari’s account also requires a verbal clause, since ‘qad’ applies only to verbs; the author says this restriction causes no difficulty because ‘qad’ cannot directly precede nouns.

SAMIN-DURR:76:1/r9.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:76:1/r9.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:76:1/r9.claim: ‘Lam yakun’ is more plausibly a circumstantial clause modifying ‘al-insan’; alternatively it is an adjective of ‘hin’ after another adjective, with an implied ‘fihi’.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p285/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p285/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p285/r1.claim: The Meccan surah was among those the Prophet recited in Friday dawn prayer, together with al-Sajda, according to a report in Sahih Muslim.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p285/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p285/r2.speaker: ابن زيد
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p285/r2.claim: Ibn Zayd gives a strange mursal report that a Black man died after hearing the surah’s description of Paradise; the Prophet said longing for Paradise had taken his life.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p259#2/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p259#2/r1.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p259#2/r1.claim: The opening rebukes the notion that humanity is left without command or purpose: although people once were not mentioned, after creation they are always significant, and the favored human cannot simply disappear without resurrection.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p259#2/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p259#2/r2.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p259#2/r2.claim: Dahr means time, which al-Razi defines as the measure of the celestial sphere's motion; the passage argues that time and creation are ordered with humanity in view, making resurrection fitting.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p259#2/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p259#2/r3.speaker: ابن مسعود
BIQAI-FULL:v8p259#2/r3.claim: Ibn Masud says Adam was made from earth and then remained in stages of clay, shaped clay, and altered dark clay for forty years each before being formed after 160 years.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p259#2/r4.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p259#2/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
BIQAI-FULL:v8p259#2/r4.claim: Al-Baghawi quotes Ibn Abbas as saying Adam was formed after 120 years rather than the 160 years attributed to Ibn Masud.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p259#2/r5.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p259#2/r5.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p259#2/r5.claim: A man recited the verse before Ibn Masud, who responded, 'I wish that had not been,' expressing dread at humanity's former insignificance.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p259#2/r6.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p259#2/r6.speaker: أبو جعفر بن الزبير
BIQAI-FULL:v8p259#2/r6.claim: Abu Jaʿfar ibn al-Zubayr says the verse recalls humanity's humble beginnings to prevent pride and the false belief that divine favors are personally deserved.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p259#s076/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p259#s076/r1.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p259#s076/r1.claim: The surah warns humanity about judgment after all creatures are gathered, with disobedient people punished in fire and obedient people rewarded in gardens amid long, terrifying scenes; its names point to human origin and fate.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p259#s076/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p259#s076/r2.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p259#s076/r2.claim: The names al-Insan, Hal Ata, al-Amshaj, and al-Dahr all signal the surah's central concern with humanity's beginning and end.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p260/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p260/r1.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p260/r1.claim: Biqāʿī places the passage after the deniers’ prideful rejection of resurrection, contrasting that posture with reflection on humanity’s humble origin.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p261/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p261/r1.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p261/r1.claim: The Creator formed varied bones, joints, tendons, and ligaments, specifying their shapes and counts so the body can move and remain sound.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p261/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p261/r2.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p261/r2.claim: Distinct senses and organs serve precise purposes: eyes convey images, ears gather sound, the nose detects scents, teeth divide food, and the tongue expresses thought.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p261/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p261/r3.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p261/r3.claim: Internal organs divide the work of digestion and circulation; the entire intricate body begins as a tiny drop in three layers of darkness, proving its unseen Maker.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p261/r4.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p261/r4.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p261/r4.claim: People marvel at a fine design on a wall yet overlook the Creator of the far greater wonders in themselves and others.

DURR-FULL:v8p365/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p365/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v8p365/r1.claim: One report from Ibn Abbas says Surat al-Insan was revealed in Mecca.

DURR-FULL:v8p365/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p365/r2.speaker: عبد الله بن الزبير
DURR-FULL:v8p365/r2.claim: Ibn al-Zubayr says Surat Hal Ata was revealed in Mecca.

DURR-FULL:v8p365/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p365/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v8p365/r3.claim: Another report from Ibn Abbas places the revelation of Surat al-Insan in Medina, differing from the Meccan reports.

DURR-FULL:v8p365/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p365/r4.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
DURR-FULL:v8p365/r4.claim: Ibn Umar reports an Ethiopian man asking whether faith and matching the Prophet's deeds would bring him to Paradise; the Prophet affirmed, promised divine reward, and the man died longing for the promised vision.

DURR-FULL:v8p365/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p365/r5.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
DURR-FULL:v8p365/r5.claim: A trusted-source report says a black man asked often about praise of God; when the Prophet recited the Paradise description in this surah, the man sighed and died of longing for Paradise.

DURR-FULL:v8p365/r6.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p365/r6.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
DURR-FULL:v8p365/r6.claim: Ibn Zayd tells of a black man who died after sighing at the surah's description of Paradise; the Prophet said longing for Paradise had taken his soul.

DURR-FULL:v8p366/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p366/r1.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
DURR-FULL:v8p366/r1.claim: Al-Hakim authenticates Abu Dharr's report that, after reciting the surah, the Prophet described the heavens creaking with angels, each space of four fingers containing a prostrating angel; knowing this would make people weep and abandon worldly pleasure.

DURR-FULL:v8p366/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p366/r2.speaker: قتادة
DURR-FULL:v8p366/r2.claim: Qatada says the human being had a period of existence before creation.

DURR-FULL:v8p366/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p366/r3.speaker: قتادة
DURR-FULL:v8p366/r3.claim: Qatada says humanity was created recently, and no creature came after humankind.

DURR-FULL:v8p366/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p366/r4.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
DURR-FULL:v8p366/r4.claim: When Umar heard the verse, he wished that it were complete.

DURR-FULL:v8p366/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p366/r5.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
DURR-FULL:v8p366/r5.claim: Ibn Masud likewise wished the verse were complete, then picked up a twig and said he wished he were like it.

DURR-FULL:v8p366/r6.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p366/r6.speaker: قتادة
DURR-FULL:v8p366/r6.claim: Qatada says Adam was the last of creation.

DURR-FULL:v8p366/r7.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p366/r7.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v8p366/r7.claim: Ibn Abbas says al-insan means every human being.

DURR-FULL:v8p366/r8.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p366/r8.speaker: عكرمة
DURR-FULL:v8p366/r8.claim: Ikrima says there are periods no one can know; no one knows how long passed before God created the human being.

DURR-FULL:v8p366/r9.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p366/r9.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
DURR-FULL:v8p366/r9.claim: After reciting the verse, Umar exclaims that God made the human being hearing, seeing, alive, and dead.

BURSEVI:v10p200#2/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p200#2/r1.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v10p200#2/r1.claim: Hal ata is a rhetorical question for affirmation and drawing the past near: hal means qad, while the implied hamza secures the listener’s admission; a real question of God is impossible.

BURSEVI:v10p200#2/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p200#2/r2.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v10p200#2/r2.claim: The phrase “a time” refers to the human species; because Adam was not made from a drop, the species means Adam’s descendants or includes him by generalization.

BURSEVI:v10p200#2/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p200#2/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
BURSEVI:v10p200#2/r3.claim: Ibn Abbas takes the unspecified span of time as the nine months a person remains in the womb before becoming a human being mentioned among people.

BURSEVI:v10p200#2/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p200#2/r4.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v10p200#2/r4.claim: Before becoming a mentioned human, the person was an unremembered drop in the loins; the pre-eternal world of spirits does not make one socially mentioned before embodiment.

BURSEVI:v10p200#2/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p200#2/r5.speaker: أبو بكر أو عمر
BURSEVI:v10p200#2/r5.claim: A report says Abu Bakr or Umar wept on hearing the verse and wished the unmentioned stage had continued, so that the person had never been created or charged with duties.

BURSEVI:v10p200#2/r6.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p200#2/r6.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v10p200#2/r6.claim: The question makes resurrection undeniable to its rejecters: the One who brought a person into being after nonexistence can restore them after death.

BURSEVI:v10p200#2/r7.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p200#2/r7.speaker: القاشاني
BURSEVI:v10p200#2/r7.claim: Al-Qashani says the person existed in divine knowledge and in reality through an eternal spirit, but was unmentioned among people while in the unseen.

ALUSI-FULL:v29p150#4/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v29p150#4/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v29p150#4/r1.claim: One analysis derives هل from أهل and treats the question as confirmation directed at a denier: people acknowledge a time when humanity did not yet exist, which supports the possibility of resurrection.

ALUSI-FULL:v29p150#4/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v29p150#4/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v29p150#4/r2.claim: هل may mean قد with a sense of drawing the past close to the present; after replacing the hamza, it combines the force of both particles.

ALUSI-FULL:v29p150#4/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v29p150#4/r3.speaker: زيد الخيل
ALUSI-FULL:v29p150#4/r3.claim: The author cites Zayd al-Khayl's verse as evidence for the construction of هل.

ALUSI-FULL:v29p150#5/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v29p150#5/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v29p150#5/r1.claim: An alternative treats هل as an ordinary question without approximation; the hamza in the cited line may add emphasis, though al-Sirafi says the correct version has أم هل and a break meaning بل.

ALUSI-FULL:v29p150#5/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v29p150#5/r2.speaker: ابن عباس وقتادة
ALUSI-FULL:v29p150#5/r2.claim: Ibn Abbas and Qatada say هل here means قد; major grammarians explain it as approximation, while others call it confirmation, and Abu Ubayda paraphrases the clause as قد أتى.

ALUSI-FULL:v29p150#5/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v29p150#5/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v29p150#5/r3.claim: The intended force of those who gloss it as قد is likely confirmatory rather than a literal replacement of one particle by another.

ALUSI-FULL:v29p150#5/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v29p150#5/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
ALUSI-FULL:v29p150#5/r4.claim: A report from Ibn Abbas identifies الإنسان with humanity as a whole.

ALUSI-FULL:v29p150#5/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v29p150#5/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v29p150#5/r5.claim: A حين is a bounded interval, whereas دهر is unbounded time, from the entire duration of the world to any unspecified long period.

ALUSI-FULL:v29p150#5/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v29p150#5/r6.speaker: أبو حنيفة
ALUSI-FULL:v29p150#5/r6.claim: Abu Hanifa hesitates to assign a conventional duration to دهر in an oath; absent an intention, his school uses the swearer's lifetime.

ALUSI-FULL:v29p150#5/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v29p150#5/r7.speaker: أبو يوسف ومحمد
ALUSI-FULL:v29p150#5/r7.claim: Abu Yusuf and Muhammad treat an indefinite dahr like حين; the text also records a six-month conventional duration for زمان absent an intention.

ALUSI-FULL:v29p150#5/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v29p150#5/r8.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v29p150#5/r8.claim: A popular story attributes differing oath rulings to the four caliphs in the Prophet's time and cites the companions-as-stars report.

ELMALILI:76:1-4#2/r1.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:76:1-4#2/r1.speaker: author
ELMALILI:76:1-4#2/r1.claim: “Ḥīn” is a bounded period, short or long, unlike “dahr,” which can denote the whole.

ELMALILI:76:1-4#2/r2.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:76:1-4#2/r2.speaker: author
ELMALILI:76:1-4#2/r2.claim: The period runs from the universe’s creation to humanity’s creation; it is bounded but its length is unknown relative to humans, and mankind came long after the universe.

ELMALILI:76:1-4#2/r3.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:76:1-4#2/r3.speaker: author
ELMALILI:76:1-4#2/r3.claim: “There was nothing mentioned” is grammatically a circumstantial clause of “human” or an adjective of “period”; the negation targets being mentioned, not existence itself.

ELMALILI:76:1-4#2/r30.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:76:1-4#2/r30.speaker: author
ELMALILI:76:1-4#2/r30.claim: These verses condense humanity’s delayed creation, successive refinement, spiritual nature, dependence on the Creator, and destiny under a law of testing and responsibility.

ELMALILI:76:1-4#2/r31.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:76:1-4#2/r31.speaker: author
ELMALILI:76:1-4#2/r31.claim: Although death does not exhaust human destiny, the human travels toward the Lord and toward either the Fire or bliss, as stated in 75:30 and 75:12.

ELMALILI:76:1-4#2/r4.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:76:1-4#2/r4.speaker: author
ELMALILI:76:1-4#2/r4.claim: Before humankind appeared as a recognized name and concept, there were precursor things, but nothing yet known or conceived as the human genus.

ELMALILI:76:1-4#2/r5.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:76:1-4#2/r5.speaker: author
ELMALILI:76:1-4#2/r5.claim: “Madhkūr” may derive from dhikr or dhukr; because the point is the concept and referent rather than merely saying “human,” the latter derivation is more apt, though the former is broader.

ELMALILI:76:1-4#2/r6.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:76:1-4#2/r6.speaker: author
ELMALILI:76:1-4#2/r6.claim: Humanity’s precursors pass through elements and minerals, then plant and animal nourishment, and finally semen, linking the account to 23:12.

ELMALILI:76:1-4#2/r7.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:76:1-4#2/r7.speaker: author
ELMALILI:76:1-4#2/r7.claim: The human genus is originated and contingent, not eternal; it came into being much later than the universe.

ELMALILI:76:1-4/r1.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:76:1-4/r1.speaker: author
ELMALILI:76:1-4/r1.claim: “Hal” can function as negation (“not”), but here interpreters take it as “qad,” affirming that the event truly or nearly came.

ELMALILI:76:1-4/r2.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:76:1-4/r2.speaker: author
ELMALILI:76:1-4/r2.claim: The affirmative sense works either as verification/proximity (“truly came” or “nearly came”) or as a rhetorical question whose answer is “yes, it came.”

ELMALILI:76:1-4/r3.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:76:1-4/r3.speaker: author
ELMALILI:76:1-4/r3.claim: The opening emphasizes that humankind appeared late in the history of creation, then explains gradual development, testing, and the divergent fates of unbelievers and the righteous.

ELMALILI:76:1-4/r4.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:76:1-4/r4.speaker: author
ELMALILI:76:1-4/r4.claim: Although some take “human” as Adam or Adam’s descendants, the evident sense is the human genus, including every individual.

ELMALILI:76:1-4/r5.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:76:1-4/r5.speaker: author
ELMALILI:76:1-4/r5.claim: Following Raghib, “dahr” in its primary sense is the total duration from the universe’s beginning to its end, and can also mean long, indefinite spans.

ELMALILI:76:1-4/r6.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:76:1-4/r6.speaker: author
ELMALILI:76:1-4/r6.claim: Unlike “dahr,” “zamān” can refer to durations both short and long, including the whole sequence of time or its parts; “dahr” denotes the whole or great spans, not an hour, day, or month.

ELMALILI:76:1-4/r7.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:76:1-4/r7.speaker: author
ELMALILI:76:1-4/r7.claim: Companions and jurists disagreed over the minimum duration meant by definite or indefinite “dahr” in oath law; Abu Hanifa suspended judgment on the indefinite form and said he did not know.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p369/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p369/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p369/r1.claim: The surah was called ‘Hal ata ala al-insan’ in the Prophet's Companions' era; other names include al-Insan, al-Dahr, al-Amshaj, and al-Abrar, though the last is reported only by al-Tabrisi.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p369/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p369/r2.speaker: أبو هريرة
IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p369/r2.claim: Al-Bukhari reports that the Prophet recited alif-lam-mim al-sajda and Hal ata al-insan in the dawn prayer.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p369/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p369/r3.speaker: ابن عباس وابن أبي طلحة وقتادة ومقاتل
IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p369/r3.claim: These authorities hold that the surah is Meccan; Ibn Masud's codex arrangement also supports that classification.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p369/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p369/r4.speaker: مجاهد عن ابن عباس وجابر بن زيد
IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p369/r4.claim: This reported view classifies the surah as Medinan; Qatada is also reported to have held this view.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p369/r6.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p369/r6.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p369/r6.claim: The surah is more likely Meccan because its style and themes match Meccan revelation; reports about verse 8 prompted the Medinan classification but may be later applications mistaken for occasions of revelation.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p372/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p372/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p372/r1.claim: The sentence may be parsed as a circumstantial clause from ‘the human,’ with its resumptive pronoun omitted.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p372/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p372/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p372/r2.claim: A ‘thing’ is an existent; ‘mentioned’ means specifically identified and named, not merely categorized, so the verse describes a person not yet existing as a distinct individual.

TABATABAI:76:1-22#2/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:76:1-22#2/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
TABATABAI:76:1-22#2/r1.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas reports that sura openings revealed in Mecca were written there and could later be extended; the report lists the early Meccan and Medinan suras, placing al-Insan among the Medinan revelations.

TABATABAI:76:1-22#2/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:76:1-22#2/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
TABATABAI:76:1-22#2/r2.claim: A report through Mujahid from Ibn ʿAbbas gives a similar revelation order and adds al-Fatiha, al-Aʿraf, and Maryam to the Meccan suras missing from the other lists.

TABATABAI:76:1-22#2/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:76:1-22#2/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
TABATABAI:76:1-22#2/r3.claim: A report in al-Durr al-Manthur from Ibn ʿAbbas says al-Insan was revealed in Medina.

TABATABAI:76:1-22#3/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:76:1-22#3/r2.speaker: علي
TABATABAI:76:1-22#3/r2.claim: In a report from Saʿid ibn al-Musayyib, ʿAli asks the Prophet about the reward for each sura and receives a revelation order that places al-Insan among the Medinan revelations.

TABATABAI:76:1-22#4/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:76:1-22#4/r1.speaker: رسول الله
TABATABAI:76:1-22#4/r1.claim: A report about an Ethiopian man says the Prophet promised him Paradise if he believed and acted as he did, described great rewards for declarations of faith and praise, and said his eyes would see the Prophet's vision in Paradise; he later died and the Prophet lowered him into his grave.

TABATABAI:76:1-22#4/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:76:1-22#4/r2.speaker: محمد بن مطرف
TABATABAI:76:1-22#4/r2.claim: A report in Ahmad's al-Zuhd says a black man died longing for Paradise after the Prophet recited the sura and described its gardens.

TABATABAI:76:1-22#4/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:76:1-22#4/r3.speaker: ابن زيد
TABATABAI:76:1-22#4/r3.claim: Ibn Zayd reports another black man died from longing for Paradise when the Prophet recited this sura.

TABATABAI:76:1-22#4/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:76:1-22#4/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:76:1-22#4/r4.claim: Even if sound, these stories show the sura's revelation coincided with the episodes, not that the episodes caused revelation; Ibn ʿUmar's presence suggests a Medinan event, compatible with revelation about the Prophet's household.

TABATABAI:76:1-22#4/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:76:1-22#4/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
TABATABAI:76:1-22#4/r5.claim: A report from Ibn ʿAbbas says the sura was revealed in Mecca.

TABATABAI:76:1-22#4/r6.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:76:1-22#4/r6.speaker: author
TABATABAI:76:1-22#4/r6.claim: The Meccan report is a summary of a longer report and conflicts with numerous reports from Ibn ʿAbbas that the sura was Medinan and revealed concerning the Prophet's household.

TABATABAI:76:1-22#5/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:76:1-22#5/r2.speaker: بعضهم
TABATABAI:76:1-22#5/r2.claim: An opposing view favors a Meccan date because the sura is early, depicts sensory rewards and punishment at length, and commands the Prophet to be patient during persecution.

TABATABAI:76:1-22#5/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:76:1-22#5/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:76:1-22#5/r3.claim: Sensory descriptions do not establish a Meccan date: the Medinan suras al-Rahman and al-Hajj contain even more extensive descriptions of reward and punishment.

TABATABAI:76:1-22#6/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:76:1-22#6/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:76:1-22#6/r1.claim: The verse is reportedly Medinan and parallels 52:48 in meaning and a closely similar context.

TABATABAI:76:1-22#6/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:76:1-22#6/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:76:1-22#6/r2.claim: The Prophet's abuse by hypocrites, diseased-hearted people, and weak believers was no less than the abuse by Meccan polytheists, as his biography shows.

TABATABAI:76:1-22#6/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:76:1-22#6/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:76:1-22#6/r3.claim: Sin and disbelief are not confined to Meccan polytheists; other unbelievers existed, and the Qur'an also attributes sin to groups of Muslims.

TABATABAI:76:1-22#6/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:76:1-22#6/r4.speaker: محمد الباقر
TABATABAI:76:1-22#6/r4.claim: Asked about “not a mentioned thing,” al-Baqir says the human was something but was not mentioned.

TABATABAI:76:1-22#6/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:76:1-22#6/r5.speaker: جعفر الصادق
TABATABAI:76:1-22#6/r5.claim: Al-Sadiq gives the same explanation: the human existed but was not mentioned.

TABATABAI:76:1-22#6/r6.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:76:1-22#6/r6.speaker: محمد الباقر
TABATABAI:76:1-22#6/r6.claim: Al-Baqir says the human was known in divine knowledge, but not yet present in creation; the author explains that he then became created and publicly mentioned.

TABATABAI:76:1-22#6/r7.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:76:1-22#6/r7.speaker: جعفر الصادق
TABATABAI:76:1-22#6/r7.claim: A report from al-Sadiq calls the human decreed but unmentioned; the author says this agrees with the preceding report.

TABATABAI:76:1-22#6/r8.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:76:1-22#6/r8.speaker: author
TABATABAI:76:1-22#6/r8.claim: The Qummi reports distinguish human knowledge from God's knowledge: one says the person was in neither knowledge nor remembrance, meaning among people; another says he was in God's knowledge but unmentioned among people.

TABATABAI:76:1-22#7/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:76:1-22#7/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:76:1-22#7/r1.claim: Although the verses may suggest that spirit and body are two separate realities, with life when joined and death when separated, the person taken at death is the whole human, not one part of a composite.

TABATABAI:76:1-22#7/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:76:1-22#7/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:76:1-22#7/r2.claim: Breathing spirit into the body makes that very body a human being; it does not join two independently distinct entities, so the human remains one reality with or without bodily attachment.

TABATABAI:76:1-22#7/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:76:1-22#7/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:76:1-22#7/r3.claim: In 23:12–14, the same drop develops through the stages of clot, lump, bones, and flesh before becoming a new creation, supporting human continuity through transformation.

TABATABAI:76:1-22#7/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:76:1-22#7/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:76:1-22#7/r4.claim: The qualification “mentioned” implies that the human was already something, such as earth or a drop, but was not yet mentioned as this particular person; he then became himself.

TABATABAI:76:1-22#7/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:76:1-22#7/r5.speaker: author
TABATABAI:76:1-22#7/r5.claim: The human is one real entity and the sole source of bodily and spiritual effects, yet is immaterial in himself, as verses about the soul's taking indicate.

ASAD-NOTES:76:1#n1/r1.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:76:1#n1/r1.speaker: classical commentators
ASAD-NOTES:76:1#n1/r1.claim: The classical commentators take hal positively as qad: an immensely long or endless span of time has indeed passed.

ASAD-NOTES:76:1#n1/r2.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:76:1#n1/r2.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:76:1#n1/r2.claim: Asad says the same sense can be conveyed by inserting 'not' into the question.

ASAD-NOTES:76:1#n2/r1.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:76:1#n2/r1.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:76:1#n2/r1.claim: A 'thing mentionable' means nonexistent even as a hypothetical concept, refuting the anthropocentric claim that man rather than a Supreme Being is life's center and ultimate reality.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p86/r1.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p86/r1.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p86/r1.claim: This surah pairs with Qiyamah and its first three verses dovetail with that surah's last four; both establish Judgment, though with different arguments.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p86/r2.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p86/r2.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p86/r2.claim: Qiyamah argues from the inward reproaching soul, whereas this surah argues from human creation and the need to reward gratitude and punish ingratitude.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p86/r3.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p86/r3.speaker: some maṣāḥif
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p86/r3.claim: Some muṣḥafs classify the surah as Medinan.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p86/r4.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p86/r4.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p86/r4.claim: Islahi rejects a Medinan classification for every verse, saying subject matter is the criterion and this surah's subject confirms it is wholly Meccan.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p86/r5.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p86/r5.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p86/r5.claim: For a time man was nonexistent; God created him from a drop through stages into a hearing, understanding being, endowed with awareness of good and evil and tested for gratitude.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:76:1/r1.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:76:1/r1.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:76:1/r1.claim: Insān derives from ins, meaning human beings as a rational, speaking, social species; the Quran treats humanity's creation, nature, and purpose in many passages.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:76:1/r2.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:76:1/r2.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:76:1/r2.claim: The Quran uses insan 65 times, ins 18 times, insī once, enāsī once, and nās 230 times.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:76:1/r3.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:76:1/r3.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:76:1/r3.claim: The passage reminds resurrection-deniers of humanity's prior nonexistence and origin so they will reflect on creation.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:76:1/r4.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:76:1/r4.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:76:1/r4.claim: Ḥīn is a bounded period and dahr unbounded absolute time; the verse concerns the interval from the world's creation to humanity's creation.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:76:1/r5.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:76:1/r5.speaker: Elmalılı
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:76:1/r5.claim: Elmalılı says the indefinite hīn is a limited but humanly unknown span between creation of the universe and humanity, when humans were not yet something named or known.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p297/r1.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p297/r1.speaker: قسم من المفسرين
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p297/r1.claim: One group identifies the human as Adam, who existed as clay before the spirit was breathed into him, but was not yet mentioned.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p297/r2.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p297/r2.speaker: قسم آخر من المفسرين
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p297/r2.claim: Another group identifies the human as Adam's descendants: each existed in the womb as something, though not yet mentioned, and was made from a mixed drop.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p297/r3.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p297/r3.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p297/r3.claim: The author prefers that al-insan denote humankind generally, including Adam and his descendants.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p297/r4.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p297/r4.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p297/r4.claim: The phrase can negate existence altogether, meaning the human was nothing in any sense; the author compares this broad negation with expressions that deny asking altogether.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p297/r5.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p297/r5.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p297/r5.claim: Alternatively, it can negate only being mentioned: the human already existed but had not yet been spoken of, as in a construction that negates play rather than creation.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p298/r1.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p298/r1.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p298/r1.claim: Mentioning مذكورا marks the stages from nonexistence to existence without mention and then the mixed drop, matching the surah's account of human development.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p298/r2.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p298/r2.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p298/r2.claim: Maryam omits مذكورا because Zakariyya's story stresses creation from absolute nothingness, a greater sign of power than creating through parents; adding it would weaken that point.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p298/r3.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p298/r3.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p298/r3.claim: The verse about human resurrection likewise omits مذكورا because it addresses people denying resurrection; absolute nonexistence makes the argument from initial creation stronger.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p299/r1.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p299/r1.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p299/r1.claim: The Qur'an uses atā for an easier arrival and jāʾa for a harder one; the human's passage into this state carries no such burden, so atā is apt.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p299/r2.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p299/r2.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p299/r2.claim: Fronting على الإنسان keeps the human, the surah's subject, in focus rather than the passing age.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p300/r1.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p300/r1.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p300/r1.claim: The author identifies the first verse's human as Adam and the next verse's human as Adam's descendants, whose creation from a mixed drop shows divine power and continued human generation.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p359/r1.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p359/r1.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p359/r1.claim: The surah traces humanity from before its beginning through its final fate, forming a journey across human life and explaining its title.

STUDYQURAN:76:1/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:76:1/r1.speaker: R
STUDYQURAN:76:1/r1.claim: In verses 1–2, man may refer to Adam, all humanity, or both.

STUDYQURAN:76:1/r2.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:76:1/r2.speaker: Qu
STUDYQURAN:76:1/r2.claim: As a rhetorical question, the verse may mean that human beings have never been unknown to God.

STUDYQURAN:76:1/r3.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:76:1/r3.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:76:1/r3.claim: Alternatively, the rhetorical question emphasizes that humanity once did not exist.

STUDYQURAN:76:1/r4.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:76:1/r4.speaker: JJ, Q, R, Ṭs
STUDYQURAN:76:1/r4.claim: With the alternative translation “There has come upon man,” most interpreters mean the period when Adam was not yet fully formed.

STUDYQURAN:76:1/r5.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:76:1/r5.speaker: R
STUDYQURAN:76:1/r5.claim: The alternative translation may instead refer broadly to the time before humanity existed.

STUDYQURAN:76:intro/r2.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:76:intro/r2.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:76:intro/r2.claim: The surah takes its title from the mention of man in its first verse.
